ety.text: From Middle English roten, from Old Norse rotinn (“decayed, rotten”), past participle of an unrecorded verb related to Old Norse rotna (“to rot”) and Old English rotian (“to rot”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rutāną (“to rot”). See rot. By surface analysis, rot + -en (past participle).

senses.d: Of perishable items, overridden with bacteria and other infectious agents.
ex: If you leave a bin unattended for a few weeks, the rubbish inside will turn rotten.

senses.d: In a state of decay.
ex: The floors were damaged and the walls were rotten.
His mouth stank and his teeth were rotten.

senses.d: Cruel, mean or immoral.
ex: That man is a rotten father.
This rotten policy will create more injustice in this country.

senses.d: Bad or terrible.
ex: Why is the weather always rotten in this city?
It was a rotten idea to take the boat out today.

senses.d: Of stone or rock, crumbling or friable; in a loose or disintegrated state.
Very drunk, intoxicated.
To an extreme degree.
ex: That kid is spoilt rotten.
The girls fancy him something rotten.

senses.d: To suffer decomposition due to biological action, especially by fungi or bacteria.
ex: The apple left in the cupboard all that time had started to rot.
Fix'd like a plant on his peculiar spot, / To draw nutrition, propagate, and rot.

senses.d: To decline in function or utility.
ex: Your brain will rot if you spend so much time on the computer, Tony!

senses.d: To (cause to) deteriorate in any way, as in morals; to corrupt.
To make putrid; to cause to be wholly or partially decomposed by natural processes.
ex: to rot vegetable fiber

senses.d: To spend a long period of time (in an unpleasant place or state).
ex: to rot in prison
to rot in Hell

senses.d: To expose, as flax, to a process of maceration, etc., for the purpose of separating the fiber; to ret.
To talk nonsense.
ex:
“Did they hang you well?” said Porson.
“Don’t rot,” said Mr Watkins; “I don’t like it.”

senses.d: Damn; blast.
The process of becoming rotten; putrefaction.
Decaying matter.
ex: When a turkey vulture detects the scent of rot, it circles down, tracing the plume of chemicals to its source.

senses.d: Any of several diseases in which breakdown of tissue occurs.
ex: His cattle must of rot and murrain die.

senses.d: Verbal nonsense.
ex: You're talking rot! I don't believe a word.

senses.d: The act of turning around a centre or an axis.
ex: The earth's rotation about its axis is responsible for its being slightly oblate rather than a sphere.

senses.d: A single complete cycle around a centre or an axis.
ex: Earth's moon completes a rotation every twenty-seven days or so.

senses.d: A regular variation in a sequence, such as to even out wear, or people taking turns in a task; a duty roster.
ex: Applying crop rotation to a field avoids depleting soil nutrients the way repeated use of a single crop might do.
In rotation, each member of the group would be responsible for the beacon fire.

senses.d: Тhe movement of investments between different sectors of an economy, or styles of investing, based on anticipated changes in the economic or market cycle.
An operation on a metric space that is a continuous isometry and fixes at least one point.
ex: The function mapping (x,y) to (−y,x) is a rotation.

senses.d: The set of starting pitchers of a team.
The step during takeoff when the pilot commands the vehicle to lift the nose wheel off the ground during the takeoff roll. (see also: V2)
Repeated play of songs on a radio station, advertisements on a television channel, etc.
ex: The new single enjoyed heavy rotation on MTV.

senses.d: To advance through a sequence; to take turns.

senses.d: To spin, turn, or revolve something.

senses.d: To advance something through a sequence; to allocate or deploy in turns.
